ex01: An object starts with { and ends with }. Inside, write key: value pairs separated by commas.
The title and the author are strings, so they need quotes. The number of pages doesn't.
ex02: Each part of the description is a property of `book`, read with a dot.
A template literal makes it easy to mix the properties with the fixed text.
ex03: The name of the property you need is inside the variable `field`.
Dot notation looks for a property literally called "field". Brackets use the value of the variable instead.
ex04: Adding and changing a property look the same: assign a value with =.
To remove a property, write the `delete` keyword followed by the property.
ex05: Checking the value isn't enough: false, 0 and undefined are all falsy, but the key exists.
There is an operator that checks whether a key exists in an object. Its name is a short English word.
Object.hasOwn also works. It receives the object and the key.
ex06: Two objects created separately are different objects, even if they look the same.
`c` doesn't copy `a`: both variables point to the same object.
Changing the object through `c` changes what `a` sees too. `b` is a separate object.
ex07: Object.keys gives you an array with the keys.
Arrays have a method that joins all the elements into one string, with a separator of your choice.
ex08: Start a total at 0, then add to it inside the loop.
for...in gives you each key. Use brackets to read the value of that key.
ex09: Start with an empty array and push one string per property.
Each entry is a pair [key, value]. Destructuring can split it into two variables right in the loop.
ex10: The name is inside `customer`, the rest is inside `address`.
Chain the dots: first the outer object, then the inner property.
ex11: Put ?. at the point where something might be missing: the address.
?. gives undefined when the address is missing. What operator turns undefined into a fallback?
ex12: Go through the products one by one and compare each product's name with `name`.
Return as soon as you find a match. If the loop ends without a match, return null.
ex13: Start a total at 0 and go through the items one by one.
Each item adds its price multiplied by its quantity.
ex14: Start with an empty object and go through the word one letter at a time.
The first time a letter shows up, it has no counter yet. Handle that case before adding 1.
The ?? operator can turn a missing counter into 0.
ex15: Methods are written inside the object, like properties, separated by commas.
Inside a method, `this` is the player. Use it to read and change the score.
addPoints needs to change the score first, and then return it.
ex16: One line with const and curly braces can create name, age and city at once.
Inside the destructuring, `= value` after a name sets its default when the property is missing.
ex17: Create a new object with { } and spread both objects inside it.
The order matters: the object written last wins when keys repeat.
ex18: `product` points to the caller's object. Changing its price changes their product too.
Create a copy with the spread operator and change the price on the copy instead.
You can copy and replace the price in the same object literal: the property written last wins.
ex19: Split the problem in two: first count every word, then find the biggest counter.
Make the text lowercase before splitting it into words.
For ties, only replace the current winner when a word has strictly more, and check the words in the order they appeared.
ex20: Start with the report object already shaped, with zeros and empty containers, then fill it in one loop.
For each product, update every part of the report: the stock, the value, its category counter and maybe the out-of-stock list.
Counting categories works like counting letters: a counter per key, created the first time.
